title: Subprograms: procedures and functions
specPoints: 2.2.3 The use of **sub programs (functions and procedures)** to produce structured code
Define and call procedures and functions; pass **parameters**; **return** values from functions; local and global variables
OCR pseudocode: `procedure name(params) … endprocedure`, `function name(params) … return x … endfunction`; Python: `def`
learn: Explain the difference between a procedure (does something) and a function (returns a value)
Define a subprogram with parameters and call it with arguments
Use `return` and store or use the returned value
Explain why subprograms make code easier to write, test, read and reuse
Distinguish local from global variables and explain why local is preferred
hook: Your quiz program prints a line of 30 dashes before and after every question — the same three lines, eight times. Then you decide the line should be 40 stars. Eight edits, and you miss one. A subprogram is writing it once, naming it, and calling the name.

video.title: Procedures and functions: name a job, then call it
video.brief: 4 minutes. Repeated code highlighted in three places, then collapsed into one `def draw_line():` and three calls. Then a parameter: `draw_line(40)` passes a value in. Then a function: `def area(w, h): return w * h` — show the value travelling back out of the function into `a = area(3, 4)`. Procedure = does; function = gives back. End with local vs global: a variable inside the function fading away when it ends.

p: A **subprogram** is a named block of code you can **call** whenever you need it. Benefits the exam wants you to list: write once, reuse many times; shorter programs; easier to **test** each part on its own; easier to **read** (the name says what it does); easier to **maintain** (fix a bug in one place); several people can work on different subprograms. This is decomposition (2.1.1) turned into code.
A **procedure** performs an action and does **not** return a value. **Parameters** are the inputs it needs, listed in the brackets; the values you pass when calling are the **arguments**.
explain.code:
OCR pseudocode                         Python
procedure greet(name)                  def greet(name):
    print("Hello " + name)                 print("Hello " + name)
endprocedure

greet("Ada")                           greet("Ada")
greet("Alan")                          greet("Alan")

p: A **function** works something out and **returns** a value to wherever it was called. The call can be used anywhere a value can: stored in a variable, printed, used in a condition.
explain.code:
OCR pseudocode                         Python
function area(w, h)                    def area(w, h):
    return w * h                           return w * h
endfunction

room = area(4, 5)                      room = area(4, 5)
print(area(3, 3) + area(2, 2))         print(area(3, 3) + area(2, 2))
if area(w, h) > 100 then …             if area(w, h) > 100:

p: A variable created **inside** a subprogram is **local**: it exists only while the subprogram runs and can't be seen outside. A variable created at the top level is **global** and visible everywhere. Prefer local variables and pass values in as parameters: it stops subprograms interfering with each other and makes them reusable. In Python, changing a global inside a function needs `global x` — a sign the design should probably pass a parameter and return a value instead.
explain.code:
def add_vat(price):
    vat = price * 0.2       # vat is local
    return price + vat

total = add_vat(50)         # 60.0
# print(vat)  -> error: vat does not exist out here

p: Questions give a function and ask what a call returns: trace it with the arguments substituted for the parameters. Or they ask you to *write* a function — include the definition line with parameters, the body, the `return`, and (often required) a line that calls it.

simple.h: Write it once, name it, call the name
p: A subprogram is a block of code with a name. Write it once. Then use the name whenever you need it.

simple.code:
def greet(name):
    print("Hello " + name)

greet("Ada")
greet("Alan")

p: A variable made inside a subprogram is **local**: it disappears when the subprogram finishes. Pass values in as parameters and send answers out with `return`.

keyterms.def: A named, self-contained block of code that can be called from elsewhere (procedure or function).
A subprogram that performs an action and does not return a value.
A subprogram that returns a value.
A variable in a subprogram's definition that receives a value when it is called.
The actual value passed to a parameter in a call.
The value a function sends back to the code that called it.
A variable that exists only inside the subprogram where it is created.
A variable declared outside any subprogram, visible throughout the program.

try.title: 1. Call, pass, return
p: Run it. Then: add a procedure `banner(text)` that prints the text between lines of dashes; add a function `is_even(n)` that returns True or False; use both.
try.code:
def greet(name):
    print("Hello,", name)

def area(w, h):
    return w * h

greet("Ada")
print(area(4, 5))
big = area(10, 12) > 100
print("Big room:", big)

try.title: 2. Refactor the repetition
p: This works but repeats itself. Rewrite it with one function `grade(mark)` that returns the grade letter, and one loop that calls it.
try.code:
m1 = 72
if m1 >= 70: g1 = "A"
elif m1 >= 50: g1 = "B"
else: g1 = "C"
print("Student 1:", g1)
m2 = 48
if m2 >= 70: g2 = "A"
elif m2 >= 50: g2 = "B"
else: g2 = "C"
print("Student 2:", g2)
m3 = 65
if m3 >= 70: g3 = "A"
elif m3 >= 50: g3 = "B"
else: g3 = "C"
print("Student 3:", g3)

try.title: 3. Local or global?
p: Predict the output, then run. Then explain in a comment why the second print shows what it does.
try.code:
count = 0

def add_one():
    count = 1
    print("inside:", count)

add_one()
print("outside:", count)

try.title: 4. Build a toolkit
p: Write and test: `get_number(prompt, low, high)` — asks until the user enters a whole number in range and returns it; `average(numbers)` — returns the mean of a list; `stars(n)` — prints n stars. Then use all three in a tiny program.

try.title: 5. Program Builder
instructions: Build a program from subprogram blocks and see how the main program reads when the detail is hidden inside well-named functions.

check.fb: Parameters in the definition; arguments in the call.

check.q: `x = double(4)` only makes sense if `double` is a:
check.fb: Something must come back to store in x.

check.q: A variable created inside a function is:
Which is NOT a benefit of subprograms?
check.fb: Structure, not speed, is the benefit.

exam.q: Write a function `fahrenheit(c)` that takes a temperature in Celsius and returns it in Fahrenheit (F = C × 1.8 + 32). Show a line of code that calls the function and outputs the result for 25 °C.
model: Correct function header with one parameter (1). Correct calculation (1). Value returned with `return` (1). Call with 25 and output, e.g. `print(fahrenheit(25))` (1).
exam.commentary: The fourth mark — the call — is forgotten by students who stop at `endfunction`. Read the whole question. A function that prints instead of returns loses the return mark.

exam.q: State **two** advantages of using subprograms when writing a large program.
model: Any two: code can be reused without rewriting; each subprogram can be tested separately; the program is easier to read and understand; easier to maintain / debug as changes are made in one place; different programmers can work on different subprograms (1 each).
exam.commentary: Two distinct advantages. 'Shorter' and 'reusable' are the same point — pick different ones.

exam.q: Explain the difference between a **local** variable and a **global** variable.
model: A local variable is declared inside a subprogram and can only be used within it / exists only while it runs (1); a global variable is declared outside any subprogram and can be accessed from anywhere in the program (1).
exam.commentary: Scope is the word. Add 'why local is preferred' only if asked; here it is not.

home: Rewrite your rock-paper-scissors or guessing game from an earlier lesson using at least three subprograms (e.g. `get_choice()`, `decide_winner(a, b)`, `show_score()`). Hand in both versions and three sentences on which is easier to change and why.

teacher.timing: 60 min: hook 4 · explain 14 · try 26 · check 5 · exam 8 · homework 3
misconceptions: Printing inside a function instead of returning, then trying to use the 'result'.
Defining a function and never calling it ('nothing happens').
Parameter and argument used interchangeably — acceptable in speech, but define them.
Believing changing a local changes a same-named global (Try 3).
say: 'What goes in through the brackets, what comes out through return?'
'If you can't test it on its own, it isn't a good subprogram yet.'
teacher.skip: Try 5 optional. Try 2 is the one that convinces students subprograms are worth it.
differentiation: Support: Try 2 with the `def grade(mark):` header and the first `if` provided.
Stretch: Try 4 — add default parameter values and explain what happens when an argument is omitted.
